title: Human Intelligence in the Age of AI
reflection: Which words matter most in my family, and could I say them first to the person, in my own voice?

o: The speed with which a mind can find an answer, and the facts it stores.
The part of the mind that stores the impressions from everything it has done.
The capacity to resonate with what is new, so that meaning grows.
The power to repeat what one has been taught, clearly and without any error.
questions.e: Speed and stored knowledge belong to other workers of the mind, and a machine can have a great deal of both. Buddhi is the attunement of the mind, the capacity to resonate with what is new so that the throb slows, the meaning grows and friction becomes flow. Discernment, a sense of what matters, conscience and care all follow from that clarity.
questions.c: Buddhi closes the gap between what comes in and what we hold

questions.q: A fifteen-year-old used an assistant to help with a hard idea in physics. Which sign shows it helped, rather than handed over, in Lesson 18?
o: She made her own attempt first, and can explain it afterwards without the tool.
She read the whole answer through twice, and wrote it out in her own hand.
The answer was correct, and her teacher gave it full marks.
She asked the assistant for several different ways of explaining it.
questions.e: In help, the tool serves our own closing of the gap: we make our attempt, the tool offers a hint or a different view, and we do the meeting. The signs are that one’s own attempt came first, that afterwards one can explain it without the tool, and that the meaning feels clear and one’s own. In handing over, the tool does the closing and we hold hazy words.
questions.c: Attempt first; can explain it without the tool

questions.q: Why does the lesson say that meaning is arrived at, not delivered?
o: Because tools often make errors, and so every answer has to be verified by us.
Because meaning is made when input meets the mind; only words can be handed over.
Because children learn better by effort than by being given any kind of answer.
Because meaning lies in the teacher, and a tool has no real teacher behind it.
questions.e: Meaning is jointly made, by what comes in and by the mind that meets it. Words can be handed across a table; meaning cannot. The effort of closing the gap is the very exercise by which buddhi grows, and when it is handed over again and again, a groove forms: a habit of receiving words and skipping the meeting.
questions.c: Meaning is made in the meeting, not handed across

questions.q: After a hard phone call with his son, a father is tempted to ask an assistant to write the message he should send. Which approach fits Lesson 18?
o: Send the assistant’s message as it is, since it is balanced and warm.
Wait until the next day, and then decide whether to write at all.
Ask the assistant for three versions, and choose the one that is most like his own.
Write a few rough lines of his own, and let the tool help with the polish only.
questions.e: When a message carries the relationship, a loving word, an apology or a hard truth, its heart is one’s own. A tool may polish it. A child learns a great deal from what the adult is seen to keep as their own. It is the work of a moment to begin again: write a rough few lines, and the tool, if you wish, can help with the polish.
questions.c: Keep the heart of the message your own

questions.q: “If an assistant answers a health question in a sure, fluent tone, that is good evidence that the answer is right.”
questions.e: A sure and fluent tone is a style, not evidence. For the body and for health, the physio, the doctor and the people who know the person are the check. The tool can help a young person prepare good questions for them, but it does not replace them.
questions.c: A fluent tone is a style, not evidence

questions.q: Why might a voice that only agrees with us leave us feeling more alone?
o: It gives the pleasant and leaves the gap as it was, so nothing grows.
It is too cold and formal, and so it cannot reach us at all when we are low.
It gives so much comfort that we no longer see any need of other people.
It answers too quickly, and so we have no time to think about what we really feel.
questions.e: A mirror has no difference in it, so there is nothing to close, and nothing grows. Resonance needs a different pitch, near enough to meet. The tradition’s two words are preyas, the pleasant, and śreyas, the good. The good confidant gives clarity without coldness, and kindness without flattery; other people keep us honest about ourselves.
questions.c: Upliftment, not agreement, is what we look for

questions.q: A fourteen-year-old has become withdrawn and prefers to talk to a chatbot rather than to people. Which response fits Lesson 18?
o: Take the chatbot away, since it is taking the place of the people in her life.
Leave her to it, since the chatbot is kind and always there for her.
Be someone she can turn to, and speak to a doctor or counsellor too.
Ask the chatbot’s makers whether their tool is safe for a person of her age.
questions.e: Parenting is building the relationship in which the child’s heart and mind can resonate with those of the parent: listening first, then widening the view. Dr Watson’s plain word: if a young person seems withdrawn and prefers a chatbot to people, please talk to the family doctor or a counsellor. The tool is not a place to arrive; the door at home is the safer place.
questions.c: The parent is the one a child turns to

questions.q: A young person is sent a video in which a famous singer seems to apologise for something. Which response fits Lesson 18?
o: Pass it on to friends at once, since others may wish to know the truth.
Ask where it came from, and ask someone you trust, before passing it on.
Trust it if the voice and the face seem real, since they would be hard to fake.
Ignore it, since public figures’ affairs are no business of ours.
questions.e: A voice or a face can now be made up. Before believing it or passing it on, ask where it came from, and ask someone you trust. That pause is buddhi at work.
questions.c: Pause, ask where it came from, ask someone you trust

questions.q: “Once a young person has handed over much of their thinking to a tool, the faculty cannot be restored.”
questions.e: What is weakened through disuse is strengthened through practice, and it is never too late to begin. The warmth that connects us may thin when meaning is handed over, and it can be restored. Practices such as repeating a mantra, sitting quietly and steady attention are ways of training this capacity, at any age.

questions.q: A parent of a fourteen-year-old wants small habits at home that keep her thinking alive when she uses an assistant. Which set fits Lesson 18?
o: Attempt first, ask for a hint, then explain it back in her own words.
Ask for the full answer first, then check it against a textbook later.
Use it only for homework, and never for any other kind of thinking.
Use it freely, and ask the school to teach her how to spot its errors.
questions.e: A few small habits: attempt first, then ask; a hint or a question serves the learner better than an answer; explain it back in one’s own words, which shows whether the meaning has arrived. A long, unbroken stretch for reading or a task, and open questions at the table, are nearness and staying in practice. A home does not need to police; it can build rhythm.
questions.c: Attempt first, hint not answer, explain it back
